title: Interaction-Aware Embedding Optimization for Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors
authors: Clément de Terrasson de Montleau, Victor Drouin-Touchette, Wesley Coelho
abstract: Neutral atom-based quantum computers have the ability to dynamically reshape the qubit register geometry between experimental runs. This capability enables different types of problems to be mapped directly onto the hardware, significantly enhancing the efficiency of solving, for instance, complex optimization and machine learning use-cases. However, this flexibility requires finding atom positions to implement target pairwise interactions, inducing a difficult nonconvex optimization for setting up the quantum machine. In this work, we introduce a new force-directed method that targets interactions to encode the input problem on the quantum computer. Numerical results show that our new method can improve embedding feasibility and solution quality by orders of magnitude, and remains reliable on the largest instances.
summary: This paper addresses the difficult optimization problem of positioning neutral atoms to achieve specific, desired pairwise interactions for quantum computation. The authors propose BLaDE, a novel force-directed algorithm that surpasses existing methods by optimizing directly on the interaction matrix rather than just the physical distances. This advancement is crucial for scaling up quantum processors by ensuring high-fidelity mapping of complex quantum circuits onto physical hardware layouts.
main_problem: The core challenge is finding physical arrangements (atom positions) that realize a desired, complex pairwise interaction pattern ($\mathbf{Q}_{	ext{target}}$) required for quantum computation.
main_result: The proposed BLaDE algorithm significantly improves the feasibility and quality of embedding solutions compared to existing methods across various instance sizes and graph types.
method: The authors introduce BLaDE, a novel force-directed optimization method that directly minimizes the difference between the target interaction matrix and the realized interaction matrix, incorporating latent dimensions to escape local minima.
model_or_system: The work focuses on neutral-atom quantum processors utilizing optical tweezer arrays, where the system dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian involving pairwise interactions ($Q_{ij} \propto D_{ij}^{-6}$).
key_observables: Relative Frobenius error ($\lVert \mathbf{Q}_{	ext{target}} - \mathbf{Q} Vert^2 / \lVert \mathbf{Q}_{	ext{target}} Vert^2$), Unit-Disk (UD) proximity, and the fraction of solvable instances.
important_parameters: The inter-atomic interaction strength ($Q_{ij}$), the target interaction matrix ($\mathbf{Q}_{	ext{target}}$), and optimization parameters like the maximum walk distance ($	ext{d}_{	ext{max walk}}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the complex, non-convex optimization problem can be effectively navigated using a force-directed approach augmented with latent dimension exploration.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares BLaDE against other methods on weighted random instances using metrics like solved fraction and error. Figure 3 shows BLaDE's superior performance on molecular graphs, particularly in achieving Unit-Disk (UD) validity.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem (mapping target interactions to geometry) and critiques existing methods. It then details the BLaDE algorithm, which involves force calculation, latent dimension optimization, and constraint enforcement. Finally, it benchmarks BLaDE against multiple baselines on both random and molecular graph datasets.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the hardware-software interface challenge in quantum computing by providing a robust, physics-informed optimization tool for mapping abstract quantum circuits onto physical hardware constraints.

Figure 2 reports the corresponding results. The subplot 2a shows the fraction of solved instances, always at 100% except for MDS on small disconnected graphs. The plain colored regions indicate embeddings that also satisfy the imposed distance-ratio constraint. BLaDE and Greedy tend to naturally satisfy the distance-ratio constraint on denser and larger instances, especially BLaDE, and the constrained versions always satisfy it. The other methods rarely meet the distance-ratio constraint, as they do not include the constraint, and do not get it for free either.
